questions.questionText: The presence of "HTTPS" and a padlock icon in the browser address bar guarantees that a login website is legitimate and safe.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Threat actors can easily acquire free SSL/TLS certificates for fraudulent domain names, displaying HTTPS padlock icons on malicious credential-harvesting websites.

questions.questionText: Which domain name represents an example of "typosquatting"?

options.text: support.google.com
login.microsoftonline.com
login.micros0ft.com
app.slack.com

questions.explanation: login.micros0ft.com uses a zero ('0') in place of the letter 'o' so it looks like Microsoft at a glance. The other three are real domains that belong to Google, Microsoft and Slack.

questions.questionText: What is the primary objective of an email phishing attack targeting remote employees?

options.text: To test home internet connection speeds
To trick users into revealing credentials, sensitive data, or executing unauthorized actions
To automatically upgrade operating system software
To clean junk files from a local hard drive

questions.explanation: Email phishing uses deceptive messages to trick victims into sharing private credentials, executing malware, or surrendering sensitive organizational data.

questions.questionText: Why do quishing attacks often succeed when targeting remote employees?

options.text: Smartphones cannot connect to Wi-Fi networks
Scanning the QR code shifts the browsing session to a mobile device outside the company's desktop security monitoring
QR codes automatically disable smartphone antivirus apps
Mobile screens automatically encrypt all user passwords

questions.explanation: Scanning QR codes on personal phones redirects traffic outside the desktop perimeter firewalls and email monitoring systems maintained by corporate networks.

questions.questionText: You receive an email notification stating your company cloud portal requires urgent re-authentication, with a link included. What is the safest way to access the portal?

options.text: Click the link in the email, enter credentials, then log out
Open a fresh browser tab, type the verified official URL manually or use a saved bookmark
Reply to the email asking if the link is safe
Copy and paste the link into a personal social media post to ask colleagues

questions.explanation: Navigating independently via a trusted bookmark or manual URL entry completely bypasses any malicious redirects embedded in the email.

questions.questionText: When an unexpected email asks you to verify an account, the lesson recommends opening the official site independently rather than following the message link.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson recommends using a trusted bookmark or entering the official address yourself instead of following an unexpected email link.

questions.questionText: A QR code from an unexpected vendor document opens a familiar sign-in or OAuth page. Is the familiar sign-in brand alone enough reason to proceed without verifying the request?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A QR code can conceal the destination of a link. Verify an unexpected request through a trusted channel before entering credentials or granting access.

questions.questionText: A suspicious link uses slack-login-security.net while claiming to be the Slack sign-in page. Which domain trick does this example illustrate?

options.text: Typosquatting
Combosquatting
A legitimate Slack-owned sign-in domain
Caller-ID spoofing

questions.explanation: Combosquatting adds trusted-sounding words to a familiar brand name. The lesson uses slack-login-security.net as its example.

questions.questionText: You receive an unexpected email asking you to sign in through an included link to view a security update. How should you check the request?

options.text: Click the link, download the file, and scan it with a free online tool
Do not use the message link; open the organization's official portal yourself or verify the request through a known official channel
Forward the email to external contacts on LinkedIn to ask if they received it
Reply directly asking the sender for their corporate employee ID number

questions.explanation: The lesson recommends opening the official site independently or confirming an unexpected request through a known official channel.

questions.questionText: You realize you entered your password on a fake login page. Which actions are taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Change the password immediately across your corporate account and any accounts reusing that password
Report the incident through your organization's trusted IT or security channel
Clear the browser history and assume this removes a password already entered on the fake page
Wait to see whether the account shows unusual activity before reporting or changing the password

questions.explanation: The lesson advises reporting the incident and changing reused passwords. Clearing local browser history does not address a password already entered on a fake page.

questions.questionText: What does the term "Quishing" refer to in modern cybersecurity?

options.text: Sending phishing attempts via voice phone calls
Hacking smart television devices
Using malicious QR codes to conceal phishing URLs and bypass security filters
Encrypting databases using ransomware

questions.explanation: Quishing stands for QR code phishing, where malicious links are embedded in image files to bypass textual email filters.

questions.questionText: Security Email Gateways (SEGs) detect embedded QR code links just as easily as standard plain-text web links.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Traditional SEGs primarily scan textual and HTML links. Image-based QR codes often bypass standard filters because the URL is hidden inside the graphic payload.

questions.questionText: Which of the following indicators strongly suggest that an email may be a phishing attempt? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: Mismatch between the display sender name and the actual email domain address
An unexpected message pressures you to act immediately to avoid an account problem
Digitally signed calendar invites sent from verified internal team accounts
An unexpected QR code that hides a link to a sign-in page

questions.explanation: The lesson identifies sender and domain mismatches, urgency, and QR codes that conceal links as reasons to verify an unexpected message.

questions.questionText: You receive an email from IT-Support@company-desk.net stating: "Your password expires in 10 minutes. Click here to retain your current password." What should you do first?

options.text: Click the link immediately to prevent losing account access
Forward the email to your personal account so you don't lose the link
Pause, do not click the link, and verify the sender address against official internal IT contacts
Reply to the email providing your current password so IT can fix it for you

questions.explanation: You should pause and verify unrequested urgent security alerts independently through official internal channels.

questions.questionText: Which observations match the domain and QR-code warning signs taught in this lesson? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: micros0ft-verify.com replaces one character in microsoft.com
slack-login-security.net adds trusted-sounding words to a familiar brand
A browser padlock proves the site belongs to the company it names
An unexpected QR code leading to a sign-in page should be independently verified

questions.explanation: The lesson demonstrates typosquatting, combosquatting, and QR codes that conceal destinations. HTTPS indicates an encrypted connection, not a trustworthy site.

questions.questionText: A QR code in an unexpected document is labeled "View client agreement" and opens a sign-in page. Is the label alone enough reason to enter your credentials?

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A QR code can hide its destination. Verify the unexpected request with a trusted contact before entering credentials.

questions.questionText: Combosquatting involves adding words like "-security" or "-login" to legitimate brand names within a domain registration.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Combosquatting merges legitimate brand trademarks with keywords (e.g., paypal-update-center.com) to mislead recipients.

questions.questionText: Which statements about an HTTPS padlock are accurate according to the lesson? (Select ALL that apply)

options.text: It indicates an encrypted connection, but does not prove the site belongs to a trustworthy company
A counterfeit site can also use a free SSL/TLS certificate and display a padlock
It verifies that the website operator is the company named on the page
Only legitimate websites can use HTTPS

questions.explanation: The lesson explains that HTTPS protects the connection, but free SSL/TLS certificates mean a counterfeit site can display the same padlock.

questions.questionText: Why do attackers create urgency in a phishing message?

options.text: To make mail servers accept larger attachments
To pressure recipients to respond quickly without pausing to verify the request
To give recipients more time to compare the request with an official source
To hide the recipient list from other message recipients

questions.explanation: The lesson explains that urgent deadlines pressure recipients to act before checking the request independently.

questions.questionText: This lesson shows that phishing can use deceptive emails and websites as well as QR codes that hide links; it is not limited to business email.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The lesson covers deceptive email and website requests and explains how QR codes can conceal links to fake login pages.
